description: We are Dreams of X from Bangladesh building the Moon-Material Simulator. Our interactive digital twin helps design NASA's 2026 regolith-plastic composite for Moon/Mars missions. Our skills: AI/ML, Web Dev (React, FastAPI, Three.js), UI/UX, and Research. We seek Aerospace/Material Science enthusiasts, ML Engineers, 3D Devs, and our 48-hour sprint. Let's build the future Join us!
summary: Moon-Material Simulator is a free browser app for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten". It tells the stories of eight NASA machines still on the Moon and Mars, then lets you rebuild one of their parts from local dust and break it in 3D. You design a composite of Moon or Mars dust and plastic, including the bacteria-grown bioplastic NASA Glenn showed in 2026, and a physics model corrected with 1,470 audited lab values predicts eight properties, each linked to the NASA report or paper behind it. It helps engineers choose a mix before a single sample is printed, and helps students, teachers and space fans learn from NASA's real data.
details:
THE CHALLENGE: ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN NASA left machines on the Moon and Mars. We tell eight of their stories: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, the Apollo 15 rover, Apollo 17's lander and its taped fender on the Moon; Viking 1, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars. Each one is also a materials experiment that never ended. Apollo 12 brought pieces of Surveyor 3 home after 31 months on the Moon, and apart from paint darkened by dust and sunlight, nothing had seriously failed. Apollo 17 fixed a broken fender with maps and tape, because there are no spare parts on the Moon.

THE PROBLEM A broken tool on the Moon can mean a resupply launch at up to $1 million per kg (NASA Glenn, NTRS 20260007758). In September 2026 NASA Glenn showed a material that could be made on site: a biodegradable plastic (PHB) grown inside bacteria fed with CO2 or crew waste, mixed with simulated Moon and Mars dust, for brackets, wrenches and chairs. The open question is which mix to make. You can't test every combination on Earth, and you can't afford to get it wrong on the Moon.

WHAT WE BUILT A free simulator that runs in any browser, in five steps:

- Learn: spin a Moon or Mars globe built from NASA maps and open a machine's story: NASA photo, what it did, why it is still there, the materials lesson and NASA sources. A "Try it" button rebuilds one of its parts from local dust.

- Design: pick a binder (NASA's bacterial PHB, PLA, PEEK, LDPE, PEI or PPSU), a soil (lunar highlands, lunar mare, Martian) and a process (printing, injection molding, hot pressing, sintered brick); set regolith up to 92.5%, basalt fibre, grain size and temperature. Eight properties update live with uncertainty, each marked "lab-backed" or "physics estimate". One click shows the real measurements behind a number, down to the table cell in the paper.

- Test: orbit the 3D microstructure, watch it print layer by layer, then load a wrench, a shelf bracket or a shelter brick until it breaks, in the habitat, at lunar noon or lunar night. It reports the breaking load, the safety factor and whether the part bends or snaps.

- Optimize: choose a use (wrench, bracket, chair, lunar wall panel, Mars shelter block, thruster nozzle). It tests about 5,000 mixes and ranks them, most locally sourced first. It says honestly when nothing works: no plastic survives a thruster nozzle.

- Plan: compare up to four formulas and estimate the launch mass and cost saved by printing parts on site.

HOW IT WORKS We transcribed 1,470 values from 11 sources (5 NASA reports, 6 peer-reviewed or preprint studies), each tied to its page, table, row and column. Our Evidence Auditor re-found every value in its source PDF: 0 transcription errors, and 181 problems documented inside the papers themselves (swapped 0/90 degree values, MPa written for GPa, an impossible -273 C glass transition). A physics model calibrated on NASA data is corrected by a Gaussian process trained on 152 real measurements from 7 studies. Tested on mixes the model never saw, the average compressive-strength error falls from 230% (physics alone) to 34%, stiffness from 65% to 19%, density from 16% to 5%, thermal conductivity from 32% to 7%. The uncertainty is calibrated: 90% of held-out mixes fall inside the 90% band. Honest limit: 152 measurements is a small, patchy dataset, so where there is no lab data near a mix, the app says "physics estimate". Use it to explore and shortlist, not as qualified design values.

WHO IT IS FOR Engineers and mission planners who want to choose a mix before printing a single sample, and just as much students, teachers and anyone who loves rockets and space. Every number links to the NASA report or paper it comes from, so it works as a classroom tool too.

TECHNOLOGY React, Vite, three.js and Chart.js in the browser, with the models exported to run client-side (no server needed); Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, SciPy and PyMuPDF for the evidence pipeline, models and optional API; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for tests and hosting. Open source under the MIT licence.

WHAT WE WOULD BUILD NEXT The same method works for Mars. Next: a Moon site picker using an open lunar regolith database, flexural strength as a ninth property, more lab data for the sparse binders and processes, and a comparison with NASA's MISSE-23 flight results once they are published.

TEAM DREAMS OF X Five friends, one team: Mahdin Islam Mukim, Maliha Sanjana, Lamisa Yeasmin Nakia, Yousuf Abdullah and Md. Habibullah Sharif. We researched, designed, built and tested it together.

Live app: https://md8-habibullah.github.io/moon-material-simulator/
